drafts.title: $61.86 for one fast charge: what charging actually costs me at home
drafts.angle: A $61.86 Supercharger receipt has people calling EVs a scam. The honest answer is where you charge: fast charging is the road-trip price, home is where the savings live. Your own monthly number settles it.
bullets: Viral overnight debate: a Tesla fast-charge session of $61.86 for 91 kWh, about 68 cents per kWh, plus a Kia EV9 fast-charge alert.
The X story summary cites home charging around $0.18 per kWh, with owners reporting $13 to $40 a month.
Non-member Supercharger pricing is cited around $0.65 per kWh at premium sites and peak times.
Most EV savings come from charging at home; fast charging is what you pay on the road.
drafts.body: $61.86 for one fast charge. That screenshot has people saying EVs are a scam. At home I pay {my price per kWh} and my last month of charging was {my monthly charging number}. Road trips cost more, sure. How many of your charges are at home vs on the road?
drafts.framework_body:
$61.86 for one fast charge.

That receipt is all over my feed this morning, and people are using it to say EVs don't save you a dime.

Here's the thing nobody in that thread is saying. That's about 68 cents a kWh at a fast charger. That's the road-trip price. It's like buying gas at the airport. You do it when you have to.

At home I pay {my price per kWh}. My last full month of charging cost {my monthly charging number}. My last I-70 trip with fast charging cost {my last road trip charging cost}.

So yes, if every charge you do is at a fast charger, the math gets close to gas. If you can plug in at home most nights, it isn't close.

And if you can't charge at home, that's an honest answer too. Renters and apartment folks have a real gap. {my one-line take on who should and shouldn't buy an EV yet}.

{screenshot of my home charging stats}

How many of your charges happen at home vs on the road?

drafts.title: $7.7 billion: what Americans over 60 lost to scams last year
drafts.angle: Medicare open enrollment is scam season, now with AI voices that sound like real people. One simple fact stops a lot of it: Medicare cards don't expire, and Medicare doesn't cold-call for your number.
bullets: FBI IC3 2025 report: Americans 60+ reported $7.748 billion in losses, up 59% from 2024; average loss $38,500; 12,444 people lost over $100,000.
Medicare open enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7; the FCC lists Medicare phone scams with AI voices among the season's scams.
Iowa Senior Medicare Patrol (Nov 4): "new chip Medicare card" calls are fake. Medicare cards do not expire and Medicare does not call asking for your number.
International Fraud Prevention Week is Nov 15 to 21.
drafts.body: $7.7 billion. That's what Americans over 60 lost to scams last year, up 59%. Now the calls can sound like a real person. One fact to tell your folks: Medicare cards don't expire. Nobody needs your number to send a new one. What's the best scam rule your family uses?
drafts.framework_body:
$7.7 billion.

That's what Americans over 60 reported losing to scams last year, per the FBI. Up 59% in one year. The average loss was $38,500. More than 12,000 people lost over $100,000.

And right now is prime time. Medicare open enrollment runs through Dec 7, and the calls are getting better. Some use AI voices that sound like a real, friendly person.

The one I'd warn everybody about: "We're sending you the new chip Medicare card, we just need to verify your number."

There is no new chip card. Medicare cards don't expire. Medicare doesn't call you out of the blue asking for your number. If someone does, hang up.

{the scam call I got, or one someone I know got}.

AI is a tool. Scammers are using it, so we should use it too: {how I'd use AI to double-check a call or letter}.

Share this with whoever in your family answers every call.

What's the best scam rule your family uses?

drafts.title: $940,000 for 8 Superchargers: your gas station could own one
drafts.angle: Tesla is building fewer of its own chargers and selling them to businesses that set their own price. That could fill gaps like the I-70 stretch faster than waiting on Tesla. Keep it about where drivers can charge, not corporate strategy.
bullets: Q3 2026: Tesla added a net 2,108 Supercharger stalls, 41% fewer than a year earlier; sessions hit a record 69 million, up 29% (The Charge Sheet).

Supercharger for Business: host buys at least 4 posts and sets the price; Tesla services it and takes about $0.10 per kWh; a standard 8-post V4 site was about $940,000 installed (Electrek configurator, cited by The Charge Sheet).
Program now in 37 countries after Mexico and Colombia launched Nov 12 (EVwire). V4 posts up to 500 kW, 97% uptime guarantee.
Tesla built 34% of new US fast-charging ports in Q3; its share of all US ports slipped to 49.3% (Paren).
drafts.body: $940,000. That's about what a business pays to put 8 Tesla Superchargers on its lot. Tesla services them and keeps a dime per kWh. I'd love to see {a GJ or I-70 business I'd want hosting chargers} do it. Which gas stop near you should buy in?
drafts.framework_body:
$940,000.

That's about what a business pays to put 8 Tesla Superchargers on its lot.

Tesla is building fewer chargers itself this year, 41% fewer new stalls than last year. But people are using them more than ever, a record 69 million sessions last quarter.

So here's the new deal. A gas station, truck stop or restaurant buys the chargers, sets the price, and Tesla keeps them running for about a dime per kWh.

That's how gaps get filled. Not waiting on Tesla to pick your town. A local owner deciding EV drivers are customers.

On the I-70 stretch I drive, I'd love to see {a GJ or I-70 business I'd want hosting chargers} do it. {why that spot makes sense}.

drafts.title: 62% off the power bill: solar plus a battery, even in December
drafts.angle: A real randomized trial, not a sales pitch: solar plus a battery cut bills 62%, and the battery kept cutting evening grid use in December. US-household lesson: the rate plan matters as much as the hardware. Your own roof number carries it.
bullets: Centre for Net Zero and Octopus Energy trial: 708 lower-income UK households given solar and batteries.
Bills fell about 62%, about 681 pounds a year; net grid imports down 77%.
The battery cut 4 PM to 8 PM grid use 66%, and it held in December.
Half the households stayed on flat rates, which wasted much of the battery's value; the battery alone was worth about 148 pounds a year.
drafts.body: 62% off the power bill. That's what solar plus a battery did for 708 homes in a real trial. The battery still cut evening use 66% in December. My roof did {my solar production this month} and my bill was {my last bill}. Are you on a time-of-use plan?
drafts.framework_body:
62% off the power bill.

That's what solar plus a battery did for 708 lower-income homes in a real trial in the UK. Not a sales pitch. A study with a control group.

The part that surprised me: the battery kept cutting evening power use 66% even in December, when the sun barely shows up.

But here's the catch. Half those homes stayed on a flat rate. A battery on a flat rate leaves money on the table. The savings come from charging cheap and using it when power costs the most.

If you're shopping solar, ask about your rate plan before you ask about panels.
